$comment: The misconception register. Every wrong option in content/bank carries a code from this file in its `catches` field. `topic` is the topic the error belongs to; a code may still be used by an item in another topic where the same error reappears (FRAC-OF-AMOUNT in ratio, INT-SUB-ORDER in algebra). Every row is sourced, as specs/question-bank-probing-misconceptions.md §4 requires: `source.kind` is `quoted` (the error is named in the DfE/NCETM guidance, with the unit and the exact wording) or `subject-knowledge` (standard error, marked as such, with the key idea it sits under). Round two adds sources one topic at a time; a row with no `source` is round one's and is not yet trustworthy.

codes.misconception: Place-value columns are confused: a digit is read as sitting in the wrong column, so its value is wrong (tenths, hundredths, thousandths, or the integer columns).

source.unit: NCETM KS3 core concept 1.1 'Place value, estimation and rounding'; DfE Mathematics guidance: Key Stage 3, Year 7 autumn, Place value, exemplified key idea 1.1.1.2
source.quote: Students are likely familiar with place value charts and the column headings in both words (tens, ones, tenths, hundredths ...) and as decimals (10s, 1s, 0.1s, 0.01s ...) but may need to revisit column headings written as fractions and exponents.

codes.misconception: One value written in different ways - a column heading as a word, a fraction, a decimal or a power of ten - is not recognised as the same value, so 1/10, 0.1 and 10⁻¹ are treated as different sizes.
codes.example: 1/10 treated as different from 0.1, or 10⁻² read as 0.02

source.unit: NCETM KS3 core concept 1.1 'Place value, estimation and rounding'; DfE Mathematics guidance: Key Stage 3, Year 7 autumn, Place value, exemplified key idea 1.1.1.2
source.quote: Understanding that a mathematical object can have the 'same value but a different appearance' is a key understanding in maths, and students may find it challenging to recognise that a column headed as tenths, 1/10, 0.1 or 10⁻¹ will represent digits of equal value.

codes.misconception: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten is treated as adding or removing zeros rather than shifting every digit between columns, so the size is left unchanged or is wrong.

source.unit: NCETM KS3 core concept 1.1 'Place value, estimation and rounding'; DfE Mathematics guidance: Key Stage 3, Year 7 autumn, Place value, key idea 1.1.1.2
source.quote: each column value is a power of ten and ... multiplying or dividing by ten shifts digits from one column to the adjacent one

codes.misconception: The number of a unit in a number is read as the single digit in that column rather than the total count of that unit in the whole number.

source.unit: DfE Mathematics guidance: Key Stage 3, Year 7 autumn, Place value, Overview
source.quote: They need to appreciate that 43 872 has 438 hundreds; and later, that 43 872 is 438.72 hundreds or 438.72 × 100.

codes.misconception: A measure is converted between units by shifting the decimal point the wrong number of places, or a decimal part of a unit is read as a whole number of the smaller unit (2.05 kg read as 2 kg 5 g).

source.unit: NCETM KS3 core concept 1.1 'Place value, estimation and rounding'; DfE Mathematics guidance: Key Stage 3, Year 7 autumn, Place value
source.note: The guidance names 'place value in the context of measure' as a key idea and asks that measures in real-life contexts be emphasised, but it does not name this error in a Common difficulties passage. Standard subject knowledge: the conversion error the key idea guards against.

codes.misconception: A zero inside a decimal is not read as a placeholder: it is ignored, or a digit beyond it is read as though the zero were not there.

source.unit: NCETM KS3 core concept 1.1 'Place value, estimation and rounding'
source.note: Not named in a Common difficulties passage for place value; the standard error the place-value-chart structure guards against. The rounding statement 1.1.3.2 separately names the difficulty of telling when a zero digit is significant.

codes.misconception: More digits after the decimal point means a larger number.

source.unit: NCETM KS3 core concept 1.1 'Place value, estimation and rounding'
source.note: Not named in a Common difficulties passage; the classic Key Stage 2 error that the named method - compare columns, not digit counts - guards against.

source.quote: students may think that −591 is larger than −3 because it's further from zero, but agree that it's a lower value

codes.misconception: There is no number, or only one number, between two close decimals, because only the columns named are considered.
